title: In a line of four, who holds the power?
hook: The centre of three takes nearly all. In a line of four, how much do the inner two get?

knows: the centre of a 3-path takes all
Nash bargaining: each side gets its fallback plus half of what is left
doesNotKnow: that in a 4-path the inner people get 2/3, not all and not half

misconception: In a line of four, the two inner people have the same power as the centre of three, so take everything.
objective: The learner can explain why, in a line of four, each inner person's outside option depends on the other inner person's deal, so the balanced split settles at 2/3 for B and C and 1/3 for A and D.

claims.text: In the line A–B–C–D with deals A–B and C–D worth $1 each, the balanced outcome gives B and C $0.667 (two thirds) each and A and D $0.333.
claims.source: Balance: v_B = o_B + (1 − o_B)/2 with o_B = 1 − v_C (A's fallback is 0); by symmetry v = 1 − v/2, so v = 2/3. Fixed-point iteration in Demo.tsx shares() from 0.5: 0.75, 0.625, 0.6875, 0.6563 … within $0.001 of 2/3 at round 9. Re-run in node by the builder (ncm-e02). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Own node iteration v <- 1 - v/2 from 0.5: 0.75 0.625 0.6875 0.6563 0.6719 0.6641 0.6680 0.6660 0.6670 ... -> 2/3; A = 1/3. Correction to this source: within $0.001 of 2/3 at round 8 (|e8| = 1/1536), not 9, so SETTLED_AT = 8 (Demo comment '// 9' is stale; see c6).

claims.text: Each round, every pair covers both people's fallbacks and halves the rest; B's fallback is what C would leave B in a B–C deal, $1 minus C's share.
claims.source: Definition of a balanced outcome (each matched pair splits its surplus over the two outside options equally): Easley and Kleinberg (2010) ch. 12; Cook and Yamagishi (1992). Round-by-round updating is the lesson's way of showing the fixed point, a simplification; stage chip 'Model: each pair covers both fallbacks, then halves the rest'. Fact-checker confirms the definition and attribution. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Definition matches the balanced outcome (Nash bargaining split with network outside options) in Easley & Kleinberg ch. 12 'Bargaining and Power in Networks' (chapter title confirmed by search snippet of the ToC; book host blocked; section placement from my own knowledge, confident) which credits Cook & Yamagishi (1992) for the concept (from memory, not opened). Round-by-round update is disclosed on the stage chip as the lesson's model.

claims.text: B's share swings (0.75, 0.625, 0.688 …) before settling, because each inner person's fallback depends on the other inner person's share.
claims.source: Iteration values from Demo.tsx shares(); the alternation follows from v_B(next) = 1 − v_C/2 with v_B = v_C. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Reveal prints ROUNDS[1..3] = $0.750, $0.625, $0.688 (0.6875 toFixed(3) = 0.688, checked). Alternation follows from error e_r = -e_{r-1}/2.

claims.text: In a line of three, the centre's two partners have no other deal, so the centre can take nearly all.
claims.source: 3-path network exchange: the end nodes' only option is the centre, so stable outcomes give the centre the whole $1 (Easley and Kleinberg 2010 ch. 12; lesson middle-of-three-takes-all). 'Nearly all' allows for a minimum unit. Fact-checker confirms. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): 3-node path: ends have only the centre, so any stable outcome gives the centre the full $1; E&K ch. 12 (placement from own knowledge, confident: the 3-path is that chapter's opening example). 'Nearly all' is fair for experiments with minimum units.

claims.text: This is a model, the balanced-outcome rule, not a forecast of any real negotiation.
claims.source: Lesson framing. Laboratory results on 4-paths (brief claim 3) need a human source check and are kept out of learner text. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Reveal muted line reads exactly this; stage chip discloses the model.

claims.text: Reveal: B's share 'settled at $0.667 (two thirds) by round N. A kept $0.333.' (N = SETTLED_AT, renders 8.)
claims.source: Unrecorded claim found by fact-checker 2026-10-14 (pass 22). SETTLED_AT = first round within TOL = $0.001 of 2/3 = round 8 (B 0.66602), not 9 as the Demo comment says. At round 8 (where 'Run until settled' stops) the stage readout shows 'B gets $0.666' and A '$0.334', while the reveal says settled at $0.667 by round 8 and A kept $0.333. DISPUTED: the reveal contradicts what the learner just saw. Fix (builder): TOL = 0.0005 gives round 9 (B $0.667, A $0.333 on the readout), or reword to 'came within $0.001 of $0.667 by round 8'.

recall.question: In a line A–B–C–D, A–B and C–D each split $1, and each pair covers both fallbacks then halves the rest. Why doesn't B take nearly all, as the centre of a line of three would?
options: B's fallback is a deal with C, and C has a good fallback too, so B can't squeeze C
recall.why: B's outside option is whatever C would leave B, and C's is whatever B would leave C. Neither is desperate, so the split settles at 2/3 to 1/3.
